episode_thesis: Krishna Guha argues that the 10-year Treasury yield has jumped to about 5.25% because of four fundamentals (AI hyperscaler debt issuance on top of a 6% of GDP deficit, a higher neutral rate from the AI investment boom, an oil and diesel shock after the US-Iran ceasefire broke down, and uncertainty about how far the Fed will hike), amplified by the new Fed chair Kevin Walsh's removal of forward-guidance guard rails and by a failed Treasury buyback attempt to cap yields. At 5%+ the non-AI economy is already crowded out (housing first) while the AI half is less rate sensitive, so the key risk is whether equities and the wealth-funded consumer can withstand yields near 5.25%. Eisman, the host, adds that daily markets simply follow oil and the 10-year and thinks QE only inflated asset prices.

speakers.name: Krishna Guha
speakers.role: Evercore ISI vice chairman and Fed watcher (guest)
speakers.speaker_note: Guest. Views attributed to Kevin Walsh and Scott Bessent are Guha's characterisation of them (second hand), flagged as such. Recording date taken from the upload date 2026-10-05; the recording is described as recent.

worldview_premises.premise: After more than five years of above-target inflation a central bank can no longer look through supply shocks, because rising inflation expectations feed wages and prices and become self-locking; a healthy labour market gives room to hike pre-emptively as insurance.
worldview_premises.support: Explains Walsh's reasoning, which Guha partly endorses ('very defensible'); no data.

worldview_premises.premise: QE does stimulate demand: it lowers government yields and, because corporate borrowing is government yield plus spread, cuts the cost of capital; it also lifts asset values and wealth effects on consumption.
worldview_premises.support: Transmission mechanism explained; no empirical estimate offered.

worldview_premises.premise: A Fed chair who sees the economy as driven by supply (productivity, labour incentives) rather than demand will use different models and run policy differently from the new-Keynesian consensus of the past 20 years.

Central-bank communication about its reaction function makes policy more effective and lets firms plan; strong forward guidance (commit to a set number of hikes) is risky and should be an emergency tool only.
worldview_premises.support: 30-year drift of Fed communication from early Greenspan, intellectual leadership of Bernanke; Greenspan's tightening/easing bias as first guidance.

worldview_premises.premise: Markets overshoot and overreact; without Fed guidance bond markets guess the Fed's criteria, so repricings run further.
worldview_premises.support: Argument from market inefficiency in guessing a single decision-maker; no data.

worldview_premises.premise: The AI boom shifts the US from excess saving to excess investment demand, which raises the neutral rate for several years and, with a 6% deficit, crowds out other borrowers.
worldview_premises.support: Reasoning about savings and investment balance; r-star not estimated.

worldview_premises.premise: Energy shocks are larger than headline crude suggests because refined products (diesel, jet fuel) rose much more; diesel roughly doubled, like oil at about 200 dollars.
worldview_premises.support: Price comparison from the conversation; unspecified source.

worldview_premises.premise: The economy in aggregate is less rate-sensitive than before the AI boom, because AI investment and wealth effects are insensitive to borrowing costs; the non-AI economy remains rate-sensitive, with housing first.
worldview_premises.support: Evidence so far of AI resilience; mortgage rates near 7% and housing 'bombed out'.

worldview_premises.premise: Large-scale Treasury buybacks cannot cap yields in a market of about 40 trillion dollars; interventions in a government's own debt market signal weakness and can raise yields.
worldview_premises.support: Size mismatch; analogy with struggling emerging markets.

worldview_premises.premise: The crisis toolkit built under Bernanke (backstops, QE, forward guidance) worked twice and prevented a 2008-scale crisis in 2020; the post-pandemic inflation lag was forgivable and the fast catch-up produced a soft landing.
Keeping rates low for longer after the financial crisis allowed a fuller labour-market recovery, because structural issues held back the economy.
Greenspan's belief that markets self-equilibrate fostered weak financial-stability regulation that was paid for in the crisis, even though his macro management was excellent.

A tariff trade war produces an initial wave of inflation through import prices; successive shocks (tariffs, the Middle East war and oil, AI demand) stopped inflation from making the final move back to 2%.

mechanism_chains.topic: Why the 10-year yield rose from about 4.5% to about 5.25%

steps.from: AI hyperscalers issue large amounts of debt on top of a government deficit near 6% of GDP
steps.to: More borrowers compete for a given pool of savings, bidding up yields (private sector crowding out government)
Higher neutral rate (r-star) for several years

steps.from: US-Iran ceasefire breaks down; diesel roughly doubles
steps.why: Energy shock larger than crude implies

steps.from: Fed hikes with no stated roadmap
steps.to: Uncertainty about how far it will go, adding upward pressure on yields
steps.why: Without guidance bond markets guess and overshoot

mechanism_chains.evidence: 10-year yield moved from about 4.5% in July to about 5.25% at recording (host); Guha lists the four drivers and says Walsh's guidance policy amplified but did not cause the move.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: Not stated for this chain; the oil impulse may fade (Guha does not see a lasting inflation impulse from oil).

mechanism_chains.topic: Higher long yields pass first to housing and non-AI business, then to equities and the wealth-funded consumer

steps.to: Housing is crushed and non-AI businesses face crowding out
steps.why: Borrowing cost too high for ordinary firms

steps.from: AI investment returns so large that 6-9% borrowing costs matter little
steps.to: AI investment is not impaired until the 10-year reaches a 6% handle
steps.why: Expected return far above cost of funds

steps.to: AI stock price gains may come under pressure earlier than AI investment
steps.why: Valuations are more rate-sensitive than the spending

steps.to: Negative wealth effect on the top-income consumer and weaker domestic demand
steps.why: Consumption is funded by stock wealth and spent at home, while AI capex leaks abroad via imported chips

mechanism_chains.evidence: Mortgage-rate and housing activity observations; reasoning about import content of AI capex.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: Guha cannot pinpoint the yield at which growth slows because the AI economy is less rate-sensitive; no precise threshold is given beyond the 6% handle for AI investment.

mechanism_chains.topic: Treasury buybacks as a yield-capping tool

steps.from: Treasury buys long bonds with proceeds from bill issuance
steps.to: An operation twist intended to lower long yields

steps.from: Buying back old illiquid high-yield bonds
steps.to: Efficient for the Treasury but little effect on market yields
steps.why: Small and concentrated in off-the-run bonds

steps.from: A few billion dollars against a roughly 40 trillion dollar market
steps.to: Failure as a cap on yields

steps.from: Intervening in the home debt market
steps.to: May raise yields on net via a credibility cost
steps.why: Resembles the behaviour of struggling emerging markets

steps.from: Buyback uncertainty and a shift of issuance toward bills
steps.to: Two-sided risk for leveraged shorts and less expected long-bond supply
steps.why: Hedge funds cannot hold a one-way short; signalling affects long yields today

mechanism_chains.evidence: Yields rose after the announcement (10-year around 5.25%).
mechanism_chains.fails_when: Guha gives Bessent credit for backing off instead of escalating.

mechanism_chains.topic: Balance-sheet shrinkage and bank liquidity rules

steps.from: Walsh wants a smaller Fed balance sheet (about 6.5-7tn dollars, down from about 9tn)
steps.why: Abrupt sales would push long-term yields sharply higher

steps.from: Waiting for stable markets and lower yields
Reform of liquidity rules such as the LCR
steps.to: Banks hold fewer reserves and more Treasuries (probably bills)
steps.why: Adds demand for government debt and helps shrink the Fed's balance sheet

mechanism_chains.evidence: Walsh's task force on the balance sheet; regulatory work by the administration and the Fed.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: Banks may prefer bills to long bonds, so long yields might not benefit.

decision_process.practice: Read Fed policy through the chair's economic framework (supply-side versus new-Keynesian), the reaction function, balance-sheet and forward-guidance stance, and Treasury actions; track a list of drivers (AI issuance, neutral rate, oil, Fed uncertainty).
decision_process.why: These explain the yield move and what the Fed will do next.

decision_process.practice: Judge disinflation from tariff pass-through rolling out of year-over-year data and the absence of second-round effects from oil.
decision_process.why: Supports an inflation view that is relatively constructive.

decision_process.practice: Watch whether equities can tolerate 10-year yields near 5.25%; the stock market is the transmission channel to the consumer.
decision_process.why: Consumer spending is held up by wealth gains at the top.

decision_process.practice: Treat strong forward guidance as an emergency tool and prefer policy rules that are explained but not committed.
decision_process.why: A central bank should not communicate more confidence than it has.

decision_process.practice: Rate policymakers against the crisis they faced and the tools they used (Greenspan split verdict, Bernanke very high, Yellen close, Powell strong on 2020 and the catch-up, last mile blamed on Trump's trade and Middle East shocks).
decision_process.why: Frames how the current Fed's tools and risks are read.

speakers.evidence_style: Institutional knowledge and reasoning from mechanisms (transmission channels, size mismatches), supported by price and rate observations given in conversation; historical grading of Fed chairs. No backtests or quantified thresholds; he declines to give a precise yield at which growth breaks.

current_views.view: Inflation should keep falling gradually: tariff inflation is dropping out and oil is not creating a lasting impulse; a hike is cheap insurance given a healthy labour market.
current_views.reasoning: Cooler summer data, tariff price level effect rolling out, labour market in good shape.

current_views.view: Long yields are driven by AI issuance, a higher neutral rate, oil and war, and Fed uncertainty; Walsh's lack of guidance amplified the move.
current_views.reasoning: Four fundamental drivers plus missing guard rails.

current_views.view: Normal Fed funds rate over the next several years should be higher than before the AI boom.
Walsh will wait for stable bond markets and lower yields before restarting gradual balance-sheet reduction.
current_views.reasoning: An abrupt reduction would raise long yields sharply.

current_views.view: Bessent's buyback did not damp yields and probably hurt confidence on net.

Yields with a five handle already strain the non-AI economy (housing first); AI investment is impaired only around a six handle, but AI stock gains may come under pressure sooner; the consumer is exposed to a stock sell-off.
current_views.reasoning: Two-speed rate sensitivity and wealth effects.

speakers.name: Steve Eisman
speakers.speaker_note: Host who states several views of his own, mainly in questions and the wrap-up.

worldview_premises.premise: QE inflated asset prices without helping the real economy.
Daily equity market moves are driven by oil prices and the 10-year yield.
At some long-term rate the economy slows, and the market is 'getting closer to the Rubicon'.
worldview_premises.support: Asserted without a level; he does not know where the rate is.

worldview_premises.premise: A Treasury buyback of 6 billion dollars is too small against the market, like a BB gun, and Bessent lost credibility.
worldview_premises.support: Size comparison; closing remark that it has clearly failed.

mechanism_chains.topic: Possible bazooka for Treasury demand via bank liquidity rules

steps.from: Loosen the LCR so big banks need to hold less liquidity
steps.why: Treasury lacks its own bazooka; bank balance sheets could supply demand

mechanism_chains.evidence: Host's own theory, presented as untested ('hasn't happened yet').
mechanism_chains.fails_when: Guha notes banks may prefer bills to long bonds.

speakers.evidence_style: Market observation and personal opinion; defers to guest on Fed mechanics.

current_views.view: Yields have marched higher, the Bessent buyback failed, and Bessent has lost credibility; the economy slows at some unknown long-term rate that may be near.
current_views.reasoning: 10-year rose from about 4.5% to well over 5% and markets move with oil and the 10-year.

disagreements.topic: Did QE help the real economy?

positions.speaker: Steve Eisman
positions.position: QE lifted asset prices but did nothing for the real economy.

positions.speaker: Krishna Guha
positions.position: QE contributed to demand through lower yields, lower corporate cost of capital and wealth effects.

positions.speaker: Kevin Walsh (as relayed by Guha)
positions.position: QE was massively overdone and continued beyond the point where benefits exceeded costs; acceptable only in emergencies. His view of a big balance sheet is part of a smaller-government philosophy.

disagreements.topic: Forward guidance and the Fed's communication

positions.speaker: Krishna Guha
positions.position: Strong forward guidance should be an emergency tool, but general explanation of the reaction function should stay because it guards against overshooting.

positions.speaker: Kevin Walsh (as relayed by Guha)
positions.position: Dislikes forward guidance and removes broader strategy guidance too, returning to early-Greenspan opacity.

disagreements.topic: Whether Bessent's buyback could have been a meaningful yield tool

positions.speaker: Steve Eisman
positions.position: Six billion dollars against a huge market is a BB gun; a real tool would need something like looser bank liquidity rules.

positions.speaker: Krishna Guha
positions.position: Narrowly sensible but small; some two-sided-risk effect; the bank-rule route is being worked on but may favour bills.

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: Guha says the yield drivers are fundamental (AI, issuance, war, oil) while also saying the lack of guidance amplified the move; the relative contribution is not quantified.
No threshold yield is given at which growth slows; Guha offers the 6% handle for AI investment and a five handle for strain on non-AI, but calls the question 'super tough'.
Guha expects falling inflation and sees no lasting oil impulse, yet lists oil and diesel as a driver of higher yields and inflation pressure.
The debate on QE is framed as opinions; neither side cites estimates.
The statement that the yield rise is not caused by Walsh conflicts somewhat with the claim that removing guard rails let rates run rampant.

forward_looking_inputs: (reader) Observable inputs named by the speakers: the 10-year Treasury yield (5.25% now, a 6% handle as an AI-investment stress level), mortgage rates (about 7%) and housing activity, oil and diesel/jet fuel prices, the tariff effect rolling out of year-over-year inflation data, the labour market, AI hyperscaler debt issuance and the government deficit (6% of GDP), Treasury issuance mix (bills versus bonds), bank liquidity-rule reform, the stock market's reaction to yields and the Fed's next steps on forward guidance and balance-sheet reduction. Horizons: weeks for yield repricing, several years for the neutral rate.
reader_inferences: (reader) The chain implies a two-speed economy in which a sustained yield rise first hurts housing and non-AI firms, with equities and the wealth-funded consumer as the second, larger channel; a break in AI-related equities would transmit to growth quickly.
(reader) Guha's argument that opacity amplifies repricing suggests yield volatility should be higher after Fed meetings if the chair gives little guidance.
(reader) If the neutral rate has risen, Guha's inflation optimism and his call for a higher normal funds rate are compatible only if policy stays restrictive for longer.
